What the official sources say

  • Connecticut's Homeowners' Elderly/Disabled (Circuit Breaker) program gives a property tax credit to owners in residence who are 65 or older or totally disabled and whose income is under set limits. (Circuit Breaker Tax Relief Program | OPM; source)
  • The credit is up to $1,250 for married couples and $1,000 for single persons, on a graduated income scale. (Circuit Breaker Tax Relief Program | OPM; source)
  • Applications are made with the local Assessor's Office between February 1 and May 15; the credit is applied by the tax collector to the real property tax bill. (Circuit Breaker Tax Relief Program | OPM; source)
  • Statutory basis for the program is CGS 12-170aa, 12-170bb and 12-170cc. (Circuit Breaker Tax Relief Program | OPM; source)

What does homestead exemption mean in Connecticut?

In Connecticut law, a homestead exemption is a shield against creditors. It is not a discount on the property tax bill. The rule sits in the postjudgment chapter of the General Statutes, section 52-352b, and it limits what a judgment creditor can reach in a home.

People often search for the phrase hoping to lower a tax bill, so the two ideas are worth separating. Tax relief for older, disabled, blind or veteran owners comes from other statutes with other names, covered further down.

How much of a home is protected from creditors?

The current statute protects the homestead of the exemptioner up to a value of $250,000. Value is the fair market value of the real property less any statutory or consensual lien on it. A smaller limit of $75,000 applies to money judgments that arise from a claim of sexual abuse or exploitation of a minor, sexual assault or other wilful, wanton or reckless misconduct by a natural person.

The amount used to be much lower. The history note under the statute shows that Public Act 93-301 first set the figure at $75,000 in 1993, that a 2003 act added $125,000 for judgments tied to hospital services, and that Public Act 21-161 replaced both with the $250,000 figure. An appellate annotation in the same chapter says the larger exemption applies in bankruptcy and postjudgment proceedings begun on or after October 1, 2021, whenever the underlying debt arose.

ItemWhat the statute says
StatuteConn. Gen. Stat. 52-352b(21)
Protected value$250,000 (fair market value minus liens)
Reduced amount$75,000 for certain misconduct judgments
Expanded exemption applies toProceedings begun on or after October 1, 2021

The statutes page notes that a 2026 supplement carries amendments passed in the 2025 sessions. Check the current text or ask a Connecticut attorney before you rely on a dollar figure.

What counts as a homestead under the statute?

A homestead is owner-occupied real property, a co-op, or a mobile manufactured home used as a primary residence. That definition is in section 52-352a(5). Co-ops were added by Public Act 10-181 and mobile manufactured homes by Public Act 94-55, according to the history note.

  • Owner-occupied: a house you rent to someone else is not a homestead for this purpose.
  • Primary residence: a second home or a vacation property does not qualify.
  • Exemptioner: the person claiming the exemption must be a natural person, so a house held in an LLC is outside the definition.

An inherited house you do not live in is not your primary residence, so the shield may not apply to it. An attorney can sort out facts like that.

Does the exemption protect a home from a mortgage or a foreclosure?

No. A mortgage is a consensual lien, and the statute measures the exemption after subtracting liens. Court annotations under section 52-352b say a mortgage is not subject to the homestead exemption, and one decision held that a waiver given voluntarily and with a lawyer's help was not against public policy.

The same annotations touch on sale proceeds. After a foreclosure sale is confirmed and reduced to proceeds, homestead exemption rights attach to those proceeds, according to one appellate ruling. Another ruling found that a trial court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to act on a homestead claim meant to protect proceeds of a voluntary sale from a judgment lien creditor.

For a homeowner who is behind on payments, that means the exemption is not a way to stop a lender. It speaks to what an unsecured creditor can take. If the problem is a mortgage in default, the options are a loan modification, a sale, or a deal with the lender, and a cash sale can close faster than a listing. Talk with an attorney or a HUD-approved housing counselor about where you stand before you sign anything.

Which Connecticut property tax breaks look like a homestead exemption?

Connecticut's exemptions for owners are listed in section 12-81 of the General Statutes, and several are fixed-dollar reductions in assessed value. The ones that most resemble a homestead exemption are tied to who the owner is.

  • Blind residents: property to the amount of $3,000 under subdivision (17).
  • Veterans who served in wartime: property to the amount of $1,000 under subdivision (19).
  • Service members and veterans with disability ratings: property up to $3,500 under subdivision (20).

The statute makes these subject to filing rules in other sections, and the exemptions also have limits when a person qualifies under more than one category. Your town assessor takes the application, so call that office for forms and deadlines. The circuit breaker credit already described on this page also runs through the assessor.

Does a tax relief program change the conveyance tax when I sell?

It can. The Department of Revenue Services lists an exemption from the state conveyance tax for the principal residence of a seller who is approved for property tax assistance under section 12-129b or 12-170aa for the current assessment year, or who was approved within the prior 15 months or less. The DRS page adds that such a deed is not exempt from the municipal portion.

The same list covers other cases that come up in distressed sales.

  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on the seller's principal residence.
  • A principal residence sold for a price too low to pay the mortgages and the tax liens that rank ahead of them.
  • A principal residence with a crumbling foundation caused by pyrrhotite, if a professional engineer has evaluated it in writing and the owner is not getting help from the Crumbling Foundations Assistance Fund. That exemption applies to the first transfer after the written evaluation.

An estate of a person who was approved for tax assistance cannot claim the first exemption.

What does the conveyance tax cost when a Connecticut house is sold?

The base state rate is three-quarters of one percent of the price, and the municipal rate is one-quarter of one percent. Both come from section 12-494. The tax applies when the consideration equals or exceeds $2,000, and the statute sets a higher state rate of one and one-quarter percent for property that is not residential, except unimproved land. Other rates apply to certain residential estates, so read the statute or ask the town clerk about a high-value sale.

PieceRate on the base caseWho receives it
State portion0.75 percentState General Fund, remitted by the town clerk
Municipal portion0.25 percentThe town's general revenue

The grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent files Form OP-236, and the tax is paid when the deed is recorded. Many towns take the return and payment online through myCTREC. In towns that do not, the grantor submits the paper form to the town clerk with a check made out to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

How do revaluations and late tax interest affect a seller?

Every Connecticut town must revalue real property at least once every five years, so a house may be reassessed at a value that looks very different from the old one. Section 12-62 sets the five-year cycle, with a schedule prescribed by the state for each revaluation zone starting October 1, 2023.

If you disagree with a new value, you can appeal to the town's board of assessment appeals. A person aggrieved by that board's action can apply to the Superior Court no later than two months after the notice of the action was mailed, under section 12-117a.

Late payments are costly. The delinquent part of a tax carries interest at 18 percent per year from the due date, with a two-dollar minimum per installment that a town may choose to waive. When a house sells, the tax collector's balance, with that interest, normally comes out of the proceeds, so it helps to ask for a payoff figure early.

What should a Connecticut owner check before selling a home with debts?

Start with a list of what is owed and what is recorded. A title search will show mortgages and recorded liens, and the town tax collector can state the property tax balance. Then match each item against the rules above.

  1. Confirm whether you live in the house as your primary residence, because that decides whether the creditor shield can apply.
  2. Ask your assessor whether you qualify for any exemption or the circuit breaker credit before the next filing window.
  3. Request a payoff from each mortgage lender and from the tax collector.
  4. Check which conveyance tax exemption, if any, matches your sale, and note its code.
  5. Speak with a Connecticut attorney if a judgment creditor is involved, since an exemption claim in court has its own procedure.

A cash sale leaves these rules as they are. It only changes the timeline and removes repairs and showings.

More questions about Connecticut Homestead Exemption

Is there a property tax homestead exemption in Connecticut?

Connecticut's statutes use the word homestead for a creditor shield of $250,000 in section 52-352b(21). Property tax relief comes from named programs such as the circuit breaker credit and the exemptions in section 12-81. Ask your town assessor which one fits you.

Can a creditor force the sale of my Connecticut home?

A judgment creditor can pursue equity above the exempt amount, and a mortgage lender is not limited by the exemption at all. The exempt value is the fair market value minus liens, so equity under $250,000 in a primary residence is protected from ordinary judgment collection. An attorney can tell you how a particular debt is treated.

Do I have to live in the house for the exemption to count?

Yes. The statute defines a homestead as owner-occupied property used as a primary residence, so a rental or a second home does not qualify. A person who inherited a house and lives elsewhere should not assume the shield applies.

Who files the conveyance tax return when I sell?

The grantor, who is the seller, or the grantor's attorney or agent files Form OP-236. It is filed and any tax paid when the deed is recorded, with the town clerk or through myCTREC if the town takes part.

Where do I apply for a veterans or blind exemption?

Apply with your town assessor. Section 12-81 sets the dollar amounts, and the assessor's office has the forms and the filing dates for your town.

title: Connecticut Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Connecticut Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Connecticut Estate and Inheritance Tax sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • For estates of decedents dying during 2026, the Connecticut estate tax exemption is $15 million. (Estate and Gift Tax Information | DRS; source)
  • Above the $15 million exemption, the tax is 12% of the excess over the federal basic exclusion amount. (Estate and Gift Tax Information | DRS; source)
  • Connecticut gift tax applies only if aggregate taxable gifts made since Jan. 1, 2005 exceed $15 million (2026 gifts). (Estate and Gift Tax Information | DRS; source)
  • Form CT-706/709 for estate tax must be filed no later than six months after the date of death unless an extension is requested (Form CT-706/709 EXT). (Estate and Gift Tax Information | DRS; source)
  • If the Connecticut taxable estate is $15 million or less, Connecticut estate and gift tax is not due. (Estate and Gift Tax Information | DRS; source)

We buy Connecticut houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What does the Connecticut estate tax actually tax?

Connecticut taxes the transfer of a dead person's estate, and the tax is imposed on the estate of each person who was a state resident at death. The rules sit in Chapter 217 of the General Statutes, mainly section 12-391.

For deaths on or after January 1, 2023, the statute sets no tax up to the federal basic exclusion amount and a 12 percent rate on the part above it. The tax payable is capped at $15 million, and that cap is reduced by Connecticut gift taxes paid since 2016.

The tax base is called the Connecticut taxable estate. For recent deaths it is the federal gross estate less allowable deductions, plus Connecticut taxable gifts made since 2005 that are not already in the gross estate, plus any Connecticut gift tax paid on gifts made in the three years before death. The state deduction for estate taxes paid is disregarded.

An executor or other filer deals with the Department of Revenue Services. The Probate Court also receives estate tax returns and return information under the chapter, and it can issue certain lien releases, as explained below.

How has the Connecticut exemption changed?

The amount of an estate that escapes Connecticut tax has risen sharply over the past several years, and it now follows the federal figure. The table shows the threshold in the statute for each year of death.

Year of deathEstate not taxed up toRate on the excess
2011 to 2017$2,000,0007.2 percent at the first bracket, rising by bracket
2018$2,600,0007.2 percent at the first bracket
2019$3,600,0007.8 percent at the first bracket
2020$5,100,00010 percent at the first bracket
2021$7,100,00010.8 percent at the first bracket
2022$9,100,00011.6 percent at the first bracket
2023 and afterFederal basic exclusion amount12 percent flat

Which exemption figure applies depends on the date of death, not the date of the sale. An heir selling a house from an estate of someone who died in 2021 follows that year's schedule, even if the closing happens years later.

The figure for 2026 deaths is stated near the top of this page from the Department of Revenue Services.

Why does the estate tax matter if you are selling an inherited house?

It matters because the estate tax is a lien in favor of Connecticut on the real property that was transferred. Under section 12-398(d), the lien runs from the due date until the tax is paid, with interest and costs.

The statute limits how far that lien reaches. It is not valid against a lienor, mortgagee, judgment creditor or bona fide purchaser until notice of it is filed or recorded in the town clerk's office or wherever such liens are recorded. A recorded notice would show up in a title search and could hold up a sale.

The statute also gives two tools for a clean closing:

  • A certificate that the tax on the transfer of the property has been paid. It can be recorded with the town clerk and is conclusive proof that the tax was paid and the lien discharged.
  • A certificate of release of lien on the decedent's interest in the real property. It can be recorded and is conclusive proof that the property is released from the lien.

An estate under the threshold owes no estate tax, and the practical task is then to get paperwork showing that nothing is due.

Who issues the certificate of release of lien in Connecticut?

The Probate Court issues it in most cases, and the Commissioner of Revenue Services issues it when the return must be filed with the Department. The statute says a person is entitled to a release when the court or the Commissioner finds, on satisfactory evidence, that payment of the tax is adequately assured or that no tax is due.

The court that acts is the probate court for the district where the decedent lived at death. If the decedent lived out of state, it is the probate court for the district where the real estate or tangible property is located.

An heir or executor planning a sale can follow this order of questions:

  • Did the decedent live in Connecticut, or only own property here?
  • Is the Connecticut taxable estate under the threshold for the year of death?
  • Does a return have to be filed with the Department of Revenue Services, which would route the release through it?
  • Has the release been recorded in the land records of the town where the house stands?

The statute also lets the Commissioner adopt regulations that set the evidence a court or the Department must see before it finds that payment is assured, so ask the probate clerk what that court expects in your case.

What if the person who died lived outside Connecticut?

Connecticut can tax the Connecticut real estate of a nonresident who died. The statute lets the state tax all real property in Connecticut and tangible personal property with an actual situs here, and it applies the tax to a fraction of the estate based on the share located in the state.

There is also a rule for houses held in an entity. For a nonresident, real property owned by a partnership, S corporation or single-member LLC is treated as personally owned by the decedent in proportion to their ownership if the entity did not carry on a profit business, the ownership was not for a valid business purpose, or the property was acquired without a bona fide sale for full consideration while the decedent kept an interest or power.

Residency itself is presumed. Section 12-391(h) says each decedent is presumed to have died a Connecticut resident, and the estate carries the burden of proving nonresidency. A filer who believes the decedent was a nonresident may request a determination of domicile after the return is filed, but only once 270 days have passed since the due date and within three years of it. The Commissioner then has 180 days to decide.

What happens if the federal estate tax figure changes later?

If the federal estate tax is changed or corrected after filing, the filer must send Connecticut an amended return within 90 days of the final determination. Section 12-398 sets that deadline, along with the rule for an amended federal return, which also triggers a 90-day amended Connecticut filing.

If the Commissioner finds additional tax due, the estate receives a notice with the extra tax and interest at 1 percent per month or fraction of a month, counted from when the original tax was due. The estate has 30 days from the mailing date to pay in cash, check, draft or money order payable to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

If instead the estate overpaid and got no federal credit for the overpayment, the State Treasurer pays the refund on order of the Comptroller. Heirs who plan to sell should keep this possibility in mind when deciding how much of the sale proceeds to hold back before distributing.

Can other people read a Connecticut estate tax return?

Generally no. Section 12-398(c) bars a probate court from disclosing estate tax returns and return information to any person or state or municipal agency, with limited exceptions.

The court must give the returns on request to the Probate Court Administrator and the Commissioner of Revenue Services. It may also share them with an executor, administrator, trustee, grantee, donee, beneficiary, surviving joint owner or other interested party who shows the court a material interest affected by the return.

For a buyer or title company, that means they will usually see a recorded certificate rather than the return itself. For an heir, it means you may need to show the court why you need access.

Does the estate tax replace property tax on the house?

No. The estate tax and local property tax are separate bills, and an inherited house keeps generating property tax while the estate is open. Under section 12-146 an unpaid tax or installment becomes delinquent after the first day of the following month and carries interest at 18 percent a year.

That interest keeps running even after a judgment for the town, and each part of a month counts as a full month. A slow estate can therefore see a property tax balance grow while the estate tax and probate steps are worked out.

Sellers of an inherited Connecticut house often need to settle several items before closing:

  • Proof from the Probate Court or the Department of Revenue Services on the estate tax lien.
  • A payoff from the town tax collector for any unpaid property tax and interest.
  • Any mortgage or other lien on the house.
  • Authority for the executor or administrator to sign the deed.

What should you ask the state before selling?

We could not confirm on an opened official page whether Connecticut charges a separate inheritance tax on heirs, so ask the Department of Revenue Services or a probate attorney before assuming the answer. The statutes read for this page impose an estate tax on the transfer of the estate.

We also did not open the Department's current filing instructions, so read the due date and extension rules above alongside the DRS form instructions.

More questions about Connecticut Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Connecticut have an estate tax?

Yes. Section 12-391 of the General Statutes taxes the transfer of the estate of a Connecticut resident, and of a nonresident's Connecticut real property.

What is the Connecticut estate tax rate?

For deaths on or after January 1, 2023, the statute sets a 12 percent rate on the part of the estate above the federal basic exclusion amount, with tax payable capped at $15 million.

Is the estate tax a lien on an inherited house?

Yes. Section 12-398(d) makes the tax a lien on the transferred real property until paid, but it is not valid against a mortgagee, judgment creditor or good-faith buyer until notice is recorded with the town clerk.

How do I get a lien release to sell an inherited house?

Ask for a certificate of release of lien. The Probate Court issues it in most cases, and the Commissioner of Revenue Services issues it when a return must be filed with the Department.

What if the estate owes more after a federal change?

The filer must send an amended return within 90 days. Additional tax carries interest at 1 percent per month and is due within 30 days of the notice.

title: Connecticut Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House
content:
Connecticut Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in Connecticut
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Connecticut Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Connecticut Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House sale
  • Turn the Connecticut Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Connecticut House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Eviction is called summary process; the first step is a Notice to Quit under CGS 47a-23, which must give at least three full days before the action is filed. (Residential Summary Process (Eviction) - Landlord; source)
  • The Notice to Quit must be served by a state marshal and include the Right to Counsel Notice (CGS 47a-75). (Residential Summary Process (Eviction) - Landlord; source)
  • A pre-termination (KAPA) notice gives 15 days to cure for certain grounds such as nuisance or material noncompliance before a Notice to Quit. (Residential Summary Process (Eviction) - Landlord; source)
  • CARES Act covered dwellings require a 30-day notice for nonpayment. (Residential Summary Process (Eviction) - Landlord; source)
  • At change of ownership the tenant must be given written notice of the name and address of the property manager (CGS 47a-6). (Landlord and Tenant Rights in Foreclosed Properties | Dept. of Banking; source)
  • Whoever owns the property when a tenant moves out must return the security deposit, even if it was paid to the prior owner (CGS 47a-21(e)). (Landlord and Tenant Rights in Foreclosed Properties | Dept. of Banking; source)
  • Cash-for-keys payments after foreclosure must be the greatest of double the security deposit plus interest, two months' rent, or $2,000 (CGS 47a-20f). (Landlord and Tenant Rights in Foreclosed Properties | Dept. of Banking; source)
  • Just cause eviction law (CGS 47a-23c) applies to buildings with five or more units; change of ownership is not cause to remove occupants aged 62+ or disabled. (Landlord and Tenant Rights in Foreclosed Properties | Dept. of Banking; source)
Selling in Connecticut?
We buy Connecticut houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What are the steps of a Connecticut eviction, from notice to court?

A Connecticut eviction, called summary process, runs through a written notice to quit, a court complaint, a judgment and then an execution carried out by a state marshal. The notice rules are in section 47a-23 of the General Statutes and the complaint rules are in 47a-23a.

The statutes already summarized above cover the notice period, the service requirements and the filing fee. This section looks at the later steps, which decide how long a landlord waits and what that means for a sale.

StageWhat the statute saysSection
Rent lateNine days of grace before a landlord may terminate for nonpayment (four days for a one-week tenancy)47a-15a
Notice to quitWritten notice giving at least three days before the quit date, with the reason stated47a-23
ComplaintMay be returnable six days, inclusive, after service, and returned to court three days before the return day47a-23a
Use and occupancyCourt may order payments while the case is pending47a-26b
After judgmentExecution stayed five days, Sundays and holidays excluded47a-35

What reasons can a landlord give in a notice to quit?

The statute lists the grounds, and the notice has to state the reason in the statutory language or words of similar import. A landlord cannot simply ask a tenant to leave. Section 47a-23 allows a notice when a lease ends and in several other situations.

  • The lease or rental agreement ends by lapse of time or by an express term.
  • The tenant violates the lease or the landlord's rules.
  • Rent goes unpaid past the grace period for residential property.
  • The tenant violates the tenant duties in section 47a-11.
  • Nuisance or serious nuisance.
  • The occupant never had a right to be there, or the right has ended.
  • An employee living in employer-furnished housing fails to leave after the job ends.

For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, a notice based on nonpayment ends the rental agreement for the period in which it is delivered and turns the tenancy into a tenancy at sufferance. The notice can also carry a use and occupancy disclaimer, which tells the tenant that any payment after the quit date is taken for use and occupancy only, with all rights reserved.

What happens once the tenant is served with a complaint?

If the tenant does not leave by the quit date, a commissioner of the Superior Court may issue a writ, summons and complaint that sets out the facts supporting immediate possession. Where a tenant appears in the case, the landlord can move for payments during the case, and the court orders them without a hearing unless the tenant objects within five days of the motion.

Section 47a-26b sets the amount at the last agreed rent, or at fair rental value when there was no agreed rent. The tenant must deposit those payments with the court within ten days of the filing of the motion. If a housing authority or another agency pays part of the rent, the requirement can be met by depositing the tenant's share.

Venue is the court location where the defendant lives or where the rental sits, at the plaintiff's choice. For a seller, the practical point is that the case moves in short steps, but a tenant who answers, asks for mediation or raises a defense can make the full timeline longer than the statutory minimum suggests.

How long does a tenant have to leave after judgment?

The tenant has a five-day stay of execution, and Sundays and legal holidays do not count toward the five days. Section 47a-35 adds that an appeal can be taken only within that five-day window, and a timely appeal stays execution until the case is finally decided unless the judge finds it was filed solely for delay or the tenant does not post the required bond.

After judgment, section 47a-42 says the defendant and any other occupant bound by the judgment must remove themselves and their possessions at once, unless a stay applies. If a stay applies, they must go when it expires. The statute goes on to cover removal and sale of unclaimed possessions.

Sections 47a-36 to 47a-41 cover other stays, and the statutes cross-reference them. A landlord who plans to sell should not set a closing date that depends on a tenant leaving until the execution date is known.

Can a landlord evict a senior or disabled tenant when the building is sold?

In larger buildings, only for the reasons the statute allows. Section 47a-23c applies to a tenant who lives in a building or complex of five or more dwelling units, or in a mobile manufactured home park, and who is 62 or older or has a qualifying disability. It also covers some tenants whose spouse, sibling, parent, grandparent or child lives with them and meets those conditions.

A landlord may bring summary process against such a tenant only for the listed grounds.

  1. Nonpayment of rent.
  2. Refusal to agree to a fair and equitable rent increase.
  3. Material noncompliance with section 47a-11 affecting health, safety or the condition of the premises.
  4. Voiding of the rental agreement, or material noncompliance with it.
  5. Material noncompliance with the landlord's lawful rules.
  6. Permanent removal of the unit from the housing market.
  7. The landlord's good-faith plan to use the unit as a principal residence.

The rent increase, removal from the market and principal residence grounds cannot be used during a lease term. Selling the building is not on the list.

What are the risks of removing a tenant without court?

The risk is real, because Connecticut has separate rules for lockouts. Chapter 833 of title 47a covers entry and detainer, and the Judicial Branch landlord and tenant page links guides on lockouts, a police training manual that addresses lockouts and self-help evictions, and a how-to for representing yourself in an entry and detainer case.

Section 47a-16 adds a limit on entry. A landlord may not enter a rented unit without the tenant's consent except in an emergency, as allowed by section 47a-16a, under a court order, or if the tenant has abandoned the unit. Entry is limited to reasonable times, apart from emergencies.

An owner who wants to sell a rented house should use the notice and court process, or reach a written agreement with the tenant. Taking shortcuts can turn a sale problem into a damages claim.

How does an eviction affect selling the house?

An open eviction case does not stop a sale, but it changes who is likely to buy and when the buyer gets possession. Buyers using a mortgage usually want vacant possession at closing, and a house with an unresolved case or a tenant holding over is harder for them.

Owners in this position usually pick one of these paths.

  • Finish the eviction, then sell vacant.
  • Sell with the tenant in place to an investor who will take over the lease.
  • Negotiate a move-out date in writing and tie the closing to it.
  • Sell as-is to a buyer who is willing to handle the tenant after closing.

Whichever path you choose, the tenant's security deposit goes with the property. Section 47a-21 treats a transfer of the landlord's interest as an assignment of the deposits, and the seller has to hand the full amount, with interest, to the new owner. The landlord and tenant law page on this site covers that rule in more detail.

Where can landlords and tenants find official help in Connecticut?

The Judicial Branch law library publishes a landlord and tenant research page with forms, a landlord's guide to summary process and a tenant's guide to eviction. It also links EvictionHelpCT.org, which describes the state's Right to Counsel program for eligible tenants, and Housing Matters information on where to file.

The Department of Housing posts mandatory landlord and tenant notice forms, a model lease and a pre-occupancy walk-through checklist. The Office of Legislative Research has reports on the eviction process, including one on recent changes (2023-R-0220), and the Judicial Branch page lists them. Because the statutes were amended after the version on the legislature's current-text page, confirm the latest wording in the 2026 supplement before relying on a deadline.

More questions about Connecticut Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How many days notice does a Connecticut landlord have to give?

Section 47a-23 requires a notice to quit that gives at least three days before the quit date, and the reason must be stated. Other rules can add time, so check the grounds that apply to your lease.

Can a tenant stay while the eviction case is pending?

Usually yes, but the court can order payments for use and occupancy under section 47a-26b if the tenant appears. The deposit is due within ten days of the filing of the motion unless the tenant objects in time.

What is the stay of execution after an eviction judgment?

Execution is stayed for five days from judgment, and Sundays and legal holidays are excluded. An appeal must be filed within those five days under section 47a-35.

Can I sell my house while a tenant is being evicted?

Yes. You can sell while a case is open, but a buyer who needs possession may wait for the execution. A cash buyer can purchase the house as-is with the tenant or the case still in place.

Where do I find the official eviction forms?

The Connecticut Judicial Branch law library page for landlord and tenant law links the summary process guides and housing forms. A Connecticut attorney can confirm which forms apply.

content:
Connecticut Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Connecticut
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Connecticut Quitclaim Deed: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Connecticut Quitclaim Deed sale
  • Turn the Connecticut Quitclaim Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Transfers between spouses are exempt from the conveyance tax. (OLR 2020-R-0020; source)
  • If property lies in more than one municipality, a conveyance tax return is completed for each town. (Real Estate Conveyance Tax Information | DRS; source)
  • Participating towns accept OP-236 filing and payment electronically via myCTREC. (Real Estate Conveyance Tax Information | DRS; source)
Selling in Connecticut?
We buy Connecticut houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Where is a Connecticut quitclaim deed recorded?

A deed goes on the land records of the town where the land lies. Section 47-10 says no conveyance is effectual to hold land against anyone except the grantor and the grantor's heirs unless it is recorded in the records of the town in which the land lies.

Connecticut has 169 municipalities, and the recording office is the clerk in the town, not a county recorder. A house in Hamden is recorded in Hamden, even though the state also groups towns into historical counties and planning regions. If the parcel sits in more than one town, ask each clerk how they want the deed handled.

An unrecorded quitclaim is a risk to both sides. The grantee may hold a paper that does not protect them against a later buyer or lender, and the grantor may still look like the owner of record when a lien or tax bill is issued.

What must a Connecticut deed contain to be valid?

Under section 47-5, a conveyance of land must be in writing, signed by the grantor, acknowledged by the grantor, and attested by two witnesses. Those formalities apply to a quitclaim deed the same way they apply to any other deed.

  • In writing, signed by the grantor or by an agent whose power of attorney was itself executed, acknowledged and witnessed as the statute requires.
  • A corporation, limited liability company or partnership signs through a duly authorized person.
  • Acknowledged as the grantor's free act and deed.
  • Attested to by two witnesses with their own hands.
  • The current mailing address of the grantee must be included.

If an agent signs under a power of attorney, section 47-10 also requires that power of attorney to be recorded with the deed, unless it is already recorded in that town and the deed refers to it. Families who use a power of attorney for a parent's house often miss that second step.

What does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Connecticut?

The fee is set by section 7-34a: ten dollars for the first page and five dollars for each additional page. The statute names a quitclaim deed among the statutory-form documents, on a form conforming to section 47-36c and titled "statutory form" in the heading, that carry the same ten and five dollar charges.

A few add-ons can raise the bill. The statute lists these extras:

SituationAdded charge under 7-34a
Deed lacks the grantee's current mailing address$5 on top of the regular fee
Names not printed or typed beneath signatures, witnesses and notary$1 on top of the regular fee
Document requiring data sent to the Office of Policy and Management under 10-261b$2 on top of the regular fee
Copy of a recorded document$1 per page; certifying a copy is $2

Other charges can apply to a deed, including the conveyance tax discussed below, so ask the clerk for a total before you mail anything.

Is there a tax on a quitclaim deed?

Possibly. The conveyance tax in section 12-494 applies to a deed or other instrument that conveys real property when the consideration equals or exceeds $2,000. The tax follows the consideration, not the name of the deed form. A quitclaim with a real price attached is taxed like any other sale deed.

The base rates are three-quarters of one percent to the state and one-quarter of one percent to the municipality. Residential value above $800,000 and non-residential use carry higher state rates. On a $250,000 transfer for value, the base charge is about $2,500 in all.

Section 12-499 explains where the money goes: the town clerk remits the state portion to the Commissioner of Revenue Services, and the municipal portion becomes general revenue of the town.

When is a quitclaim deed exempt from the conveyance tax?

Several listed transfers are exempt under section 12-498, and these come up most often with family quitclaims.

  • Deeds between spouses.
  • Deeds where the consideration is less than $2,000.
  • Transfers that change only the identity or form of ownership, with no change in beneficial ownership.
  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure that transfer the transferor's principal residence.
  • Deeds securing a debt, and deeds releasing property held as security.
  • Deeds made under certain superior court decrees named in the statute.

An exemption does not remove the deed's other costs, and it does not erase the property tax. It also does not tell you whether a transfer is wise. A gift or a no-price deed within the family can still raise questions about an existing mortgage and about the owner's own plans. Those are matters for an attorney, and the statutes cited here do not settle them.

Does a quitclaim deed fix a tax, lien or title problem?

Not by itself, and none of the statutes cited here say otherwise. A recorded tax levy, a mortgage or an unpaid municipal bill stays on the property until it is paid or released. The grantee takes the house in whatever condition the title is in.

Property tax is billed against the parcel. Under section 12-111, a person to whom title has been transferred since the assessment date can appeal the assessment, which shows that the tax system expects ownership to change hands while a year's bill is open. A new owner should find out about the October 1 assessment and any unpaid installments before closing on a quitclaim.

If the reason for the quitclaim is a divorce, an estate or a dispute among heirs, the court file or probate record may control what the deed can say. A title company can search the land records and tell you what is open.

Can I sell a house after receiving it by quitclaim?

Yes, provided the deed was properly signed, witnessed, acknowledged and recorded, and the title searches cleanly. A buyer's title company will look at how the seller took title, and a gap in recording or a missing power of attorney will surface at that point.

Sellers who got a house this way often face the same issues: back taxes, repairs, a co-owner who has not signed, or heirs who disagree. Cash buyers who purchase as-is regularly deal with these files. The first step is a clean copy of the recorded deed and the current tax bill, which together show who owns the house and what is owed on it.

If the buyer is paying in cash, closing speed depends mostly on how fast the clerk's office returns the recorded deed and how soon the payoff figures arrive. Sellers who live far from the property should ask the title company how to arrange the signing so the acknowledgment and the two witnesses meet section 47-5.

For a quick reference, three documents carry most of the weight at closing: the recorded deed, the tax collector's payoff statement and any power of attorney that was used.

More questions about Connecticut Quitclaim Deed

Where do I record a quitclaim deed in Connecticut?

With the town clerk in the town where the property is located. Section 47-10 makes recording in that town's land records what protects the grantee against third parties.

How many witnesses does a Connecticut deed need?

Two. Section 47-5 requires the deed to be in writing, signed, acknowledged by the grantor and attested to by two witnesses, and to include the grantee's current mailing address.

What is the recording fee for a Connecticut quitclaim deed?

Ten dollars for the first page and five dollars for each additional page under section 7-34a, plus any add-on charges the statute lists, such as $5 when the grantee's mailing address is missing.

Do I pay conveyance tax on a quitclaim deed?

If the consideration is $2,000 or more and no exemption applies, yes. The base rate is 0.75 percent to the state and 0.25 percent to the municipality. Deeds between spouses are exempt.

Is a power of attorney recorded with the deed?

Yes. Section 47-10 requires the power of attorney to be recorded with the deed unless it is already recorded in that town and the deed refers to it.

Does a quitclaim deed remove a tax lien?

No. A deed moves ownership and does not discharge a lien or an unpaid tax. Ask the tax collector and a title company what is open before you sign.

title: Connecticut Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the Sale
content:
Connecticut Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the Sale

Cash Home Buyers in Connecticut
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Connecticut Tax Sales: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Connecticut Tax Sales sale
  • Turn the Connecticut Tax Sales offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Connecticut House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • If not redeemed, the tax collector's deed is recorded and full title vests in the purchaser; owners are barred of their rights under 12-189. (Municipal Tax Sales (Extra-Judicial); source)
  • A collector's deed is prima facie evidence of valid title in the grantee (12-159). (Municipal Tax Sales (Extra-Judicial); source)
Selling in Connecticut?
We buy Connecticut houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Who runs a tax sale in Connecticut?

The municipal tax collector does. Connecticut has 169 municipalities, each with its own collector, and the sale procedure in section 12-157 is written for that officer.

When the collector levies a tax warrant on real estate, the collector prepares a notice with the taxpayer's name, a legal description or a citation to the land records, the street address, the amount due as of the last day of the prior month, and the date, time and place of the sale. A statement must say that more taxes, interest and fees accrue after the stated date, so the number on the notice is a floor.

Because each town runs its own sale, scheduling, bidder rules and auction practice vary. The statute lets the collector publish or announce rules for the orderly conduct of the auction, and lets the town hire auctioneers and clerks.

What happens before a house reaches a tax sale?

The usual path begins with an unpaid installment, then interest, then a written demand, and only later a levy. Each step has a statutory trigger.

StageWhat the statute provides
Installment dueTown sets one, two or four payments; last due at least 45 days before fiscal year end (12-142)
DelinquentUnpaid after the first day of the following month; interest at 18 percent per year, $2 minimum (12-146)
DemandCollector makes or sends demand when tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date (12-155)
Levy and noticeWarrant levied on real estate; notices posted; sale scheduled (12-157)
SaleAuction run by the collector; written notice of amounts due posted at the sale (12-157(d))

The sections cited above describe the levy and sale as the collector's procedure, and none of them calls for a lawsuit first. Read the notice you receive for the specific date and place.

How long do I have to redeem after a Connecticut tax sale?

The deadline is not later than six months after the date of the sale. If the property was abandoned, or meets other conditions set by a municipal ordinance, the period can be as short as sixty days. Both rules come from section 12-157(f).

The collector must give notice within sixty days after the sale. The statute calls for publication in a daily newspaper that circulates in the town and for certified mail, return receipt requested, to the delinquent taxpayer and to each mortgagee, lienholder and other encumbrancer of record whose interest is affected. The notice states the sale date, the purchaser's name and address, the price paid and the date the redemption period ends.

The notice also warns what follows if redemption does not happen by that date: titles, mortgages, liens, restraints on alienation and other encumbrances in the property are extinguished. The deed to the purchaser stays with the town clerk, unrecorded, for six months from the sale.

Who else gets notice, and why does that matter to a seller?

Mortgage holders and other lienholders receive the same notice as the owner, because their interests are on the line.

  • The delinquent taxpayer.
  • Each mortgagee of record whose interest is affected.
  • Each lienholder and other encumbrancer with a choate interest.
  • The public, through newspaper publication.

For a seller this means a tax sale is rarely a private problem. A heavy mortgage on a house with tax arrears can pull the lender into the process, and the title company will see the levy in the land records. If you have inherited the house, ask the collector which address the notices went to, so you know what was sent and when.

What can the purchaser do during the redemption period?

The purchaser has limited rights. Under section 12-157(g), during the redemption period the purchaser or the municipality has an insurable interest in the buildings and improvements and may insure them against fire and other risk of physical loss.

The purchaser or the municipality may also petition the superior court for a receiver, or for other equitable relief, if there is imminent danger of damage or destruction to the buildings, or of injury to people or other property from conditions on the lot or on neighboring properties. The statute adds that the purchaser or municipality is not liable, and does not forfeit its interest, solely because it holds the tax deed, for conditions that exist or events that occur during that period.

Ask the collector who bought at the sale and what was paid, since the post-sale notice must state both along with the date redemption ends. Those three facts are what a title company will want to see.

Can I sell before the tax sale or during the redemption period?

Yes, and a sale at either point is how many owners clear the debt. Before a sale, a buyer pays the arrears with interest and charges from the proceeds. After a sale, redemption requires payment of what the statute and collector require, and the closing has to fit inside the redemption window.

The costs on a closing statement are straightforward: the payoff, any mortgage balance, and the conveyance tax if it applies. Under section 12-494, the base rate is three-quarters of one percent to the state and one-quarter of one percent to the municipality on a sale price of $2,000 or more. Tax deeds are among the transfers section 12-498 lists as exempt, but a deed from you to a buyer is a different instrument.

Timing is the main variable. A cash buyer who buys as-is can often move on a short schedule, but a payoff statement, a title search and a signing date still take days. Start well before the sale or redemption deadline, and ask the tax collector for exact figures in writing.

Is there a way to stop a sale altogether?

The sale notice itself warns that taxes, interest and fees keep accruing after the stated amount, so any payoff has to be confirmed with the collector. This page cannot say whether your town takes partial payments or sets up a payment plan, and none of the statutes cited here require it. Ask the office.

You can also contest the underlying tax, within limits. An assessment appeal has a February 20 deadline under section 12-111, and a court application must come within two months of the board's mailed notice under section 12-117a. Neither is a way to stop a sale already scheduled, so use them for the next tax year and call the collector about this one.

Ask these at the tax office, and write down the answers with the date and the name of the person who gave them:

  • How much is owed today, with interest and fees, and the per-day or per-month increase.
  • Whether a warrant has been levied and whether a sale date has been set.
  • Whether a sale has already happened, and if so, the date it will no longer be possible to redeem.
  • The office's written procedure for paying off the account.

More questions about Connecticut Tax Sales

Who holds a tax sale in Connecticut?

The municipal tax collector. Each of the state's 169 municipalities runs its own collection and sale, following section 12-157.

How long is the redemption period after a Connecticut tax sale?

Not later than six months after the sale, or sixty days if the property was abandoned or meets conditions set by a municipal ordinance.

What notice must I get after a tax sale?

Within sixty days of the sale, the collector must publish a notice and mail one by certified mail to the taxpayer and to each affected mortgagee and lienholder.

What happens if I do not redeem?

The notice states that titles, mortgages, liens and other encumbrances in the property are extinguished if redemption does not take place by the stated date.

Can I sell my house to stop a tax sale?

Yes. The arrears, interest and charges are paid from the sale proceeds. Ask the tax collector for a written payoff figure and share it with the title company.

Does interest keep running on delinquent Connecticut property tax?

Yes. Section 12-146 sets 18 percent per year, with a $2 minimum per installment unless the town has voted not to impose it.

title: Connecticut Property Tax Guide: Appeals, Exemptions and Selling With Tax Due
content:
Connecticut Property Tax Guide: Appeals, Exemptions and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Connecticut
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Connecticut Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Connecticut Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Connecticut Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Connecticut House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

Selling in Connecticut?
We buy Connecticut houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Who bills property tax in Connecticut?

In Connecticut each town or city assesses and bills its own property tax. The state has 169 municipalities: 19 cities, 149 towns and one borough. They sit inside eight historical counties and nine planning regions, but the property tax is a municipal matter, so there is no county bill to look for.

That shapes a sale. The assessor in your town sets the value, the board of assessment appeals hears disputes, and the tax collector sends the bill and takes payment. Population runs from 785 in Union to 148,654 in Bridgeport, and the same statutes govern both. Staffing, payment options and office hours do not, so a call to your own town hall answers more than any statewide summary.

  • Assessor: values the property and keeps the grand list.
  • Board of assessment appeals: hears appeals filed by the February deadline.
  • Tax collector: bills, collects, sends demands and handles delinquent accounts.
  • Town clerk: records the deed and collects the conveyance tax at closing.

How is a Connecticut home assessed?

Every municipality uses an October 1 assessment date and assesses property at 70 percent of its present true and actual value. Both rules come from section 12-62a of the General Statutes.

The 70 percent figure trips up many owners. A house a buyer would pay $300,000 for carries an assessed value of $210,000 on the grand list. The tax bill is then built from that assessed figure, so comparing your assessment to an asking price without adjusting for the 70 percent will make the number look too low.

The October 1 date also matters for timing. The value on that date is the one used for the bill, even if you sell the next spring. A buyer who later pays the bill is working from the status of the house as of that October, not the day of closing.

How often does Connecticut revalue property?

Towns must revalue on a five-year cycle. Under section 12-62, after October 1, 2023 each town revalues not later than the October 1 that falls five years after an assessment date set by a schedule the Secretary of the Office of Policy and Management prescribes for each revaluation zone.

In practice, your town has a revaluation year on a published schedule, and in between the assessor works from the same values with changes for new construction, demolition and corrections. Revaluation years are when assessments jump or fall for whole neighborhoods at once. If you plan to list or sell to an investor the year after a revaluation, expect the new value to show up on the next bill, and expect a buyer to ask for it.

Which year applies to your address is not something a state page can tell you. The assessor's office can say when the last revaluation took effect and when the next one is due.

When is the deadline to appeal a Connecticut assessment?

An appeal to the board of assessment appeals must be filed in writing or by electronic mail on or before February 20, according to section 12-111. The appeal has to include the owner's name, a description of the property, the reason for the appeal, the owner's own estimate of value and a signature.

The statute also gives some detail that sellers and heirs miss:

  • A person to whom title has been transferred since the assessment date can file the appeal.
  • A lessee bound by a recorded lease to pay property taxes can file.
  • The board must send hearing notice no later than March 1, and at least seven calendar days before the hearing.
  • For commercial, industrial, utility or apartment property assessed over $1,000,000, the board may decline to hold a hearing and must say so by March 1.

The deadline is strict. If you inherit a house in January and the notice sits in a drawer, February 20 does not move. Ask the assessor for the form early.

Can I take an assessment dispute to court?

Yes. Under section 12-117a, a person who is aggrieved by the board's action can apply to the superior court for the judicial district not later than two months after the date the board mailed notice of its action. The application carries a citation to the town, and it is served like a summons in a civil action.

The same section lets an appellant whose appeal the board chose not to hear go directly to the superior court. For a typical single-family house, that path is rarely needed. For a seller, the practical point is the clock: two months from the mailing date, not from the date you read the letter.

Before spending money on a court case, compare the likely tax savings with the cost and with how soon you plan to sell. A house that will close in six months often does not justify a multi-year dispute, though the right to appeal can pass to the buyer in some cases. A local attorney can look at the numbers.

When are Connecticut property taxes due, and what happens if I pay late?

Each municipality decides. Section 12-142 lets the town's legislative body choose a single payment, two semiannual installments or four quarterly installments, with the last installment due no later than 45 days before the end of the fiscal year. Your town's bill states the exact dates.

Late payments cost real money. Under section 12-146, a delinquent tax bears interest at 18 percent per year, with a minimum charge of $2 per installment unless the town votes not to impose that minimum. An installment becomes delinquent after the first day of the month following the month it was due.

StepWhat the statute says
Payment scheduleOne, two or four installments, set by the town (12-142)
Interest on late tax18 percent per year, $2 minimum per installment (12-146)
Written demandCollector sends a demand if tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date (12-155)
Levy and saleCollector prepares notices and may sell the real estate (12-157)

What happens at a Connecticut closing when tax is still due?

The unpaid bill is paid from the sale proceeds, and the buyer or title company normally confirms the balance with the tax collector before the deed is recorded. Ask the collector for a current figure with interest, because a number from last month will be short.

A seller who is behind has two realistic choices. One is a sale with the arrears cleared at the table. The other is waiting, which adds interest and, in time, a demand and a levy. Demand comes first: under section 12-155 the collector sends it when a tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date. A levy and a tax sale follow if the account stays open, as the page on Connecticut tax sales explains.

An as-is cash buyer can close around these problems, because the payoff is a line item and not a financing contingency. The offer will account for the arrears; it will not ignore them.

What conveyance tax applies when I sell?

Connecticut charges a conveyance tax on a deed when the consideration is $2,000 or more. Under section 12-494, the basic state rate is three-quarters of one percent of the price, plus one-quarter of one percent that goes to the municipality.

The state rate rises for expensive homes and for non-residential property.

  • Residential, up to $800,000: 0.75 percent state rate.
  • Residential, $800,000 to $2,500,000: 1.25 percent on the part above $800,000.
  • Residential, above $2,500,000: 2.25 percent on the part above $2,500,000.
  • Property used for something other than residential use, except unimproved land: 1.25 percent.

A $400,000 house therefore owes about $3,000 at the state rate and $1,000 at the municipal rate, or $4,000 in all. Whether the buyer or seller pays is a matter of the contract and local custom, so read the purchase agreement.

Which transfers are exempt from the conveyance tax?

Section 12-498 lists many exemptions, and a few matter for ordinary owners. Deeds between spouses are exempt, tax deeds are exempt, and so are deeds securing a debt or releasing security for one. Deeds made under certain court decrees, and deeds in lieu of foreclosure that transfer the transferor's principal residence, are listed as well.

Also exempt are transfers that only change the form of ownership with no change in beneficial ownership. A sale to an investor does not fit these categories, and a seller should assume the tax applies unless the town clerk or an attorney says otherwise.

What should a seller do first?

Pull the current bill and the assessor's record for the property, then call the tax collector for a payoff figure. Next, check whether the February 20 appeal window is still open, and whether the town is in a revaluation year.

Keep copies of every notice. If a demand or a notice of levy arrives, treat the date on it as a real deadline, because the redemption period after a tax sale is short.

More questions about Connecticut Property Tax Guide

What percent of value does Connecticut assess for property tax?

Seventy percent. Section 12-62a requires municipalities to assess all property at 70 percent of present true and actual value as of October 1.

What is the deadline to appeal my Connecticut property assessment?

February 20. The appeal goes to your town's board of assessment appeals in writing or by email, and it must state the reason and your estimate of value.

Can I appeal to court after the board rules?

Yes, within two months of the date the board mailed notice of its action, by applying to the superior court for the judicial district where the town sits.

What interest do I owe on late Connecticut property tax?

Eighteen percent per year, with a $2 minimum per installment unless the town has voted not to impose that minimum.

Does the county bill my property tax?

No. The town or city assesses, bills and collects. Connecticut has eight historical counties, but the tax is assessed and collected locally.

What is the conveyance tax on a $400,000 Connecticut house?

About $4,000 at the base rates: 0.75 percent to the state and 0.25 percent to the municipality. Higher-priced homes and non-residential property pay more.

Can I sell a house with property tax unpaid?

Yes. The balance, with interest, is normally paid from the proceeds at closing. Ask the collector for a payoff figure dated near the closing.
